one_liner: Bun's built-in JavaScript HTTP server (Bun.serve); 2.0-2.2x Go net/http throughput on a 3-route hello-world API, 4 cores.
what_it_does: Bun is a JavaScript/TypeScript runtime (JavaScriptCore engine, Node.js-compatible APIs) shipped as one `bun` executable, and Bun.serve() is its native HTTP server. You pass a `routes` table (static paths, `:param` and `*` wildcard routes, per-method handlers, pre-built `Response` objects, `{ dir }` folders) plus an optional `fetch(req, server)` fallback; handlers take a Web-standard Request and return a Response or Promise<Response>, and the same server does TLS, WebSocket pub/sub, and experimental HTTP/2 and HTTP/3. It is not a drop-in for Go net/http: you rewrite handlers in JS/TS and deploy the Bun runtime, and the server is not usable as a C, C++ or Rust library.
how_it_is_fast: Sockets, parsing and routing stay in native code: uSockets (C) runs an epoll (epoll_pwait2) or kqueue loop, not io_uring, and Bun's uWebSockets fork (C++) parses requests with SWAR word-at-a-time scanning (the `hasLess` bit trick on 8-byte words, with 32 bytes of required buffer post-padding) and a Bloom filter over header names, then dispatches through uWS's tree router. The glue layer (Rust since 1.4, Zig before) takes request contexts from a pre-allocated pool of 2,048 and writes response metadata inside uWS 'corked' sections, while ServerRouteList keeps route callbacks in a fixed array and caches one JavaScriptCore Structure per route's params object so the JIT sees a single shape; params are percent-decoded with SIMD. Constant `Response` routes are served with no allocation and no JS. Multi-core throughput comes from one process per core sharing the port through `reusePort` (Linux SO_REUSEPORT), with the kernel spreading connections across them.
when_to_use: JS/TS HTTP APIs on Linux where per-request stack overhead dominates. In the 2026-09-24 the-benchmarker run on 4 cores, Bun.serve with JS route callbacks did 145,897 req/s at c=512 vs 67,239 for Go net/http, with p99 latency of 4.4 ms vs 15.5 ms.
Node.js services that want more throughput without leaving JavaScript: in the same run raw Bun.serve beat Fastify on Node (68,128 req/s) by ~2.1x and Express (42,586) by ~3.4x.

Health checks, redirects, fixed JSON and static files: constant `Response` routes are dispatched with no allocation (the docs claim at least 15% faster than returning a new Response), and `{ dir }` routes (1.4+) stream files with sendfile and handle ETag, 304 and Range.
WebSocket fan-out servers that want built-in topic pub/sub, per-socket backpressure limits and permessage-deflate without extra packages.
Linux deployments where one worker process per core behind `reusePort` (or node:cluster) is acceptable.
when_not_to_use: As a speed-only reason to leave Go: in the same run Go fasthttp (125,657 req/s) and Fiber (123,666) came within ~1.16-1.18x of Bun, and an earlier 2026-09-20 snapshot of this suite, measured differently, showed Bun only ~1.12x ahead of net/http.

macOS or Windows production, or any host without SO_REUSEPORT: `reusePort` is ignored there, and Bun's docs say node:cluster can only load-balance HTTP on Linux. You get one JS thread per server, while the Go binary in this run used 3.9 cores from a single process with no cluster code.

CPU-heavy handlers or state shared in memory across requests: each worker is a separate process with its own heap and one event-loop thread, so a slow synchronous handler stalls every connection on that worker.

gRPC, or anything that needs production HTTP/2 or HTTP/3: both are experimental in Bun.serve. There is no WebSocket over HTTP/2, no server push and no response trailers. The 1.4 notes say not to ship `http3: true` to production yet, since 0-RTT is disabled and server.upgrade() returns false over H3.

Risk-averse deployments: Bun 1.4 (2026-08-20) is the first release of a Zig-to-Rust port done mostly by Claude agent workflows in 11 days. About 4% of the Rust sits in `unsafe` blocks. Advisories for the 1.4 security fixes are held back until people upgrade, and a request-smuggling bug (issue #29732, fixed 2026-04-27) has an open request for a CVE (#30921).

integration.form: runtime built-in (Bun.serve ships inside the single `bun` executable; nothing to install beyond Bun itself, optional @types/bun for TypeScript types; cannot be linked into C/C++/Rust programs)
integration.dependencies: none beyond the bun binary, which statically links JavaScriptCore/WebKit, a uWebSockets fork, uSockets, BoringSSL, lsquic/ls-hpack/ls-qpack, mimalloc and others
integration.min_toolchain: Bun 1.4.x as benchmarked (oven/bun:1.4-slim image); `{ dir }` folder routes are new in 1.4.0; no compiler needed
integration.platforms: Linux x64/arm64 (glibc 2.17+ or musl builds; kernel 5.6+ recommended; the installation docs say 3.10 is the minimum, the README says 5.1), macOS 13+ x64/arm64, Windows 10 1809+ x64/arm64, FreeBSD 14.3+ x64/aarch64 (new in 1.4), experimental Android. x64 needs SSE4.2 (Nehalem): one binary picks AVX2/AVX-512 code paths at runtime. Multi-process port sharing (`reusePort`) works only on Linux.
integration.thread_safety: Each Bun.serve instance runs its handlers on its process's single JS event-loop thread, so handlers never run in parallel within one process. Scaling across cores means separate processes sharing the port through `reusePort` (Linux SO_REUSEPORT) or node:cluster, and HTTP load balancing across processes is Linux-only. Running Bun.serve from Worker threads is not documented as a scaling path.

gotchas: `idleTimeout` defaults to 10 s and counts a handler that is still working but has not written a byte as idle, so slow handlers see connection resets. The maximum is 255 s (open issue #15589 asks to raise it). For SSE or long streams, call `server.timeout(req, 0)` for that request.

Multi-core scaling fails silently: `reusePort` is ignored on macOS and Windows, and open issue #43690 (2026-09-21) reports that node:http `listen({ reusePort: true })` is ignored even on Bun, while node:net honours it.

Since 1.3.4, requests with malformed Content-Length, Transfer-Encoding or chunked framing get 400 and the connection is closed without calling your handler or logging anything. Check a hand-written client's framing headers first.
Constant `Response` routes are cached for the server's lifetime; call `server.reload()` to change them. WebSockets (`server.upgrade()`) work only over HTTP/1.1, so `http1: false` disables them.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick Bun.serve over fasthttp only when the service is, or should become, JS/TS: staying in Go, fasthttp reached 0.86x Bun's throughput in the same run with no runtime switch. Bun.serve is the zero-dependency base under Elysia, which scored 173,877 req/s largely because its benchmark routes are constants Bun serves natively; uWebSockets.js scored 174,621 on Node with a lower-level API, so pick it instead if you must stay on Node.
verified_claims_summary: In the-benchmarker/web-frameworks run of 2026-09-24 (commit f673364; zrk closed-loop keep-alive, 15 s per level, mean of GET /, GET /user/:id and POST /user; server pinned to cpuset 0-3 and load generator to CPUs 4-15 of a 16-CPU x86-64 Linux 7.2 host, CPU model not recorded), Bun 1.4.x (oven/bun:1.4-slim, mislabelled 1.2.5 in data.json) running Bun.serve routes as one reusePort node:cluster worker per core did 144,254 / 145,871 / 145,897 req/s at c=64/256/512 vs 71,499 / 67,382 / 67,239 for Go 1.27 net/http with http.ServeMux (go build -trimpath, GOAMD64=v3), i.e. 2.02-2.17x. p99 latency was 0.90 vs 3.05 ms at c=64 and 4.38 vs 15.51 ms at c=512; an earlier 2026-09-20 snapshot of the suite, measured differently, gave only ~1.12x.
status_note: Very active (last push 2026-09-26, v1.4.2 on 2026-09-05, 96k stars, owned by Anthropic since December 2025) and MIT for Bun's own code, but the binary statically links LGPL-2 JavaScriptCore/WebKit and LGPL-2.1 tinycc, and 1.4 is the first release of the Rust rewrite, so expect a few releases of settling.
